extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical philosophy reading Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics (with commentary/notes)
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory notes and commentary on Aristotle's Ethics (Books VI–X), discussing distinctions in types of knowledge (episteme, nous, phronesis, techne), the nature of induction, logical division, practical wisdom, akrasia, and related ethical concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes and purposes of knowledge (aplos vs eneka tinos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind attains truth either for the sake of truth itself ([Greek: aplos]), or for the sake of something further ([Greek: eneka tinos]). If the former, knowledge may be syllogistic ([Greek: episteme]), non-syllogistic ([Greek: nous]), or by a union ([Greek: sophia]). If the latter, it is directed either to action ([Greek: phronesis]) or to making ([Greek: techne]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative framing: the mind contemplates Matter Necessary or Contingent; if necessary, principles ([nous]), deductions ([episteme]) or mixed ([sophia]); if contingent, action ([phronesis]) or production ([techne]). This distinction underpins how one evaluates the aim and appropriate method of an inquiry or activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotle's definition of Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is defined as 'the proving the inherence of the major term in the middle (i.e. proving the truth of the major premiss)' through observed particulars; it presupposes a syllogism in the first figure with a universal affirmative conclusion, the universal being taken as proved by Induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canonical formulation: if of one and the same term two others be predicated, one coextensive with that term and the other not, coextensiveness must be ascertained by nous (the inductive faculty). Example: 'All Magnets attract iron' is inferred from observed A B C magnets attracting iron and nous recognizing A B C as coextensive with 'Magnets.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and limits of Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction does not imply actual examination of all particulars; it is a 'bridging over a chasm', a branch of probable reasoning whose validity depends entirely upon the quality of the particular mind performing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid induction is a mark of genius; the certainty it produces is subjective rather than objective. A syllogistic exhibition of an induction may be nugatory or hide a premiss that is literally false. Compare Aristotle's Analytica Prior II.25 and Post. Analyt. I.1,3 for context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for premises of episteme (scientific knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Premises from which episteme draws its conclusions must be 'true, first principles incapable of any syllogistic proof, better known than the conclusion, prior to it, and causes of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These conditions are the test for acceptable first principles in demonstrative/scientific reasoning (see referenced appendix). They mark what can serve as a starting point for syllogistic demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for correct logical division
rubrics_metrics.description: The correct logical division requires that the membra dividentia shall be opposed — i.e., the subdividing parts must be mutually exclusive and not included one by the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the test of a correct logical division; improper divisions where parts overlap or are nested indicate faulty definition or classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of popular/language sense and conversion as a test in definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial appeal in many definitions is to popular language; one predicates a popular name of a 'so and so' and then converts the proposition, which is the proper test of any logical definition or specific property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: calling Architecture an Art and showing the connection via conversion tests whether the logical definition or specific property holds. This approach is compared to the treatment of episteme, phronesis, and sophia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and character of Practical Wisdom (phronesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical Wisdom (phronesis) concerns means rather than ends (though it selects subordinate ends as means to the highest end); it is employed about self or not-self (domestic, community, legislation, government) and exists in both a full sense (practical wisdom) and an incomplete sense (merely the intellectual element).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phronesis often results from experience; when applied to civil government it is called Legislation, while administering functions is Government. The term is context-sensitive and admits different names for its functions (e.g., deliberation, administration of justice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation of nous (intuitive intellect) as authoritative
rubrics_metrics.description: There are principles and particular facts that cannot admit of reasoning and must be authoritatively determined by nous (the faculty which attains truth in such cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What makes nous a true guide is practice—i.e., experience. Aristotle brings both prior principles and perceptual facts within the province of nous; acceptance or rejection without proof is sometimes required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchinoia (rapid right conjecture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchinoia is 'a happy conjecture of the middle term without time to consider of it' — the rapid and correct accounting for an observed fact (e.g., the moon's bright side is next to the sun).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchinoia is contrasted with slow reasoning; it captures sudden insight about causation or the middle term that explains observed phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between opinion and deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion is a complete mental act, whereas deliberation is an incomplete mental act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction is a technical point about mental acts relevant to ethical psychology and practical reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral principle: the End does not sanctify the Means
rubrics_metrics.description: A stated moral maxim: 'The End does not sanctify the Means.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a terse ethical note; rejects the idea that achieving an end automatically justifies wrongful means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of akrasia (weakness of will) via premise-substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Akrasia is explained by the suggestion of epithymia (desire) which supplies a different minor premise at the moment of action, substituting 'This is sweet' for 'This is excess', thereby altering the syllogistic sequence and producing action contrary to prior deliberated maxim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a man with the maxim 'All excess is to be avoided' may, under temptation, accept the minor premise 'This is sweet' (suggested by desire) rather than 'This is excess' (right reason), leading to the conclusion 'This glass is to be tasted.' This accounts for failures of self-control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of moral major premises by habit (ethismos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Major Premiss of the 'Practica' syllogism is wrought into the mind by repeatedly acting upon the Minor Premiss (i.e., through habit, ethismos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: by habitually acting on 'This is pleasant' a person comes to hold the Major Premiss 'All that is pleasant is to be done.' Habituation thus shapes moral cognition and dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception of virtue's claims (rightness and expediency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue may be considered under two aspects: as being right, and as being truly expedient—Conscience and Reasonable Self-Love are two principles of moral constitution that, if properly understood, lead the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bishop Butler's treatment is cited: reasonable self-love (when properly understood) coincides with the principle of virtue and should not be disclaimed by moralists; this bears on how moral motives and expediency are evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of pleasure (instantaneous and indivisible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is an instantaneous sensation that cannot be conceived as divisible or incomplete; the longest continued pleasure is only a succession of single sparks giving the appearance of a stream.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to analyze psychological claims about pleasure and its role in action; informs evaluation of hedonistic premises in ethical reasoning.
